candidates.attacker_control: A remote client fully controls the multipart request body, including each part's Content-Disposition header value. By sending a form-data part whose name/filename parameter contains an RFC 2047 encoded-word with malformed Base64 (e.g. filename="=?utf-8?B?A?="), the client drives MimeUtils.decodeWord() down the Base64 branch with invalid input.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Base64.getMimeDecoder() ignores non-alphabet characters, so not every malformed-looking string throws; IllegalArgumentException requires structurally invalid Base64 (e.g. one leftover character or bad padding). Unsupported charset names do not take this path (they surface as UnsupportedEncodingException/IOException, which is handled). ParameterParser/RFC2231 paths catch checked exceptions as intended. The defect is bounded to one request; no cross-request state is corrupted, and a container typically converts the escaped RuntimeException into a 500 response.
candidates.impact: Denial of service / unexpected server error on attacker-crafted uploads: processing fails with an undeclared runtime exception instead of the library's checked error path, preventing applications from mapping it to a controlled 4xx and aborting parsing/cleanup semantics of the request. No confidentiality or integrity impact was established from source.
candidates.prerequisites: Application parses multipart requests with AbstractFileUpload.parseRequest()/getItemIterator() (or the servlet/portlet wrappers). No special configuration is required; the affected header is processed before any body data. The unchecked exception must not be caught by application code (the public API contract declares only FileUploadException/IOException).
candidates.root_cause: MimeUtils.decodeWord() decodes the encoded-text of an RFC 2047 encoded-word with java.util.Base64.getMimeDecoder().decode(...) (MimeUtils.java:229) inside a try block that only catches IOException (line 238). java.util.Base64 throws unchecked IllegalArgumentException for malformed Base64 (e.g. bad length/padding). decodeText() wraps decodeWord() with catch (ParseException) only (MimeUtils.java:137-156), ParameterParser.parse() wraps the call with catch (UnsupportedEncodingException) only (ParameterParser.java:177-183), and AbstractFileUpload.getFieldName()/getFileName() plus FileItemInputIteratorImpl.findNextItem() add no catch. The malformed header value is entirely attacker-controlled (Content-Disposition parameter of a multipart part), so the unchecked exception propagates out of parseRequest()/getItemIterator() instead of the declared FileUploadException or IOException.
candidates.title: Uncaught IllegalArgumentException from Base64 decoding of attacker-controlled RFC 2047 encoded words in multipart part headers
candidates.trace: Client multipart part header -> MultipartInput.readHeaders() -> AbstractFileUpload.getParsedHeaders() -> FileItemInputIteratorImpl.findNextItem() calls fileUpload.getFieldName(headers)/getFileName(headers) (lines 166, 177) -> AbstractFileUpload.getFileName()/getFieldName() -> ParameterParser.parse() line 179 -> MimeUtils.decodeText() -> decodeWord() line 229 Base64.getMimeDecoder().decode(encodedData) throws IllegalArgumentException; only IOException is caught at line 238, only ParseException at line 154, only UnsupportedEncodingException at ParameterParser line 180, so the exception escapes parseRequest()/getItemIterator().
candidates.unverified: Runtime confirmation that a specific string triggers IllegalArgumentException from the JDK decoder was not executed (source-only review). The application/container's handling of an escaped RuntimeException and the final observable severity were not verified; if callers catch RuntimeException defensively the impact drops to a stack trace/log noise. Whether upstream already tracks/fixed this specific error-handling gap is unknown (no network or history inspection was permitted).
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-248 Uncaught Exception / CWE-20 Improper Input Validation (availability impact)

coverage_summary: All 99 assigned files were within the mandatory filters (no over-size, sensitive-name, or symlink exclusions; identical filters for B0/P1). The P1 index reports 99/99 files indexed, 44 Java files parsed, 0 parse errors, but explicitly no control-flow, data-flow, semantic resolution, or Spring runtime verification, and 408 unresolved calls; index rows were used only as navigation hints and every cited edge was checked against source text. I read in full or in substantially complete line ranges: all core parsing classes (MultipartInput 1028 lines, FileItemInputIteratorImpl, FileItemInputImpl, AbstractFileUpload, ParameterParser, RFC2231Utils, MimeUtils, QuotedPrintableDecoder, DiskFileItem, DiskFileItemFactory, AbstractRequestContext, RequestContext, FileItem, FileItemFactory, FileItemInput, FileItemHeadersImpl), and the jakarta-servlet5, javax, portlet request-context/cleaner/factory classes; I inspected the root pom, changes.xml, security-reports.xml, checkstyle/pmd/spotbugs configuration, and CI workflows for vulnerability-relevant configuration. Not fully line-by-line: the exception classes, FileItemHeaders/FileItemHeadersProvider/ProgressListener, the jakarta-servlet6 and remaining javax/portlet mirrors, distribution/site files, and most module POMs; these were covered by targeted searches (count-limit, size-limit, file/path, process, sink searches) rather than complete reads.
limitations: Source-only review: no compilation, tests, container, or runtime reproduction was performed; the escaped-exception behavior and its observability depend on unexecuted JDK/container behavior.
The P1 relation index provides syntax/navigation candidates only; it does not prove reachability, data flow, or exploitability, and 408 calls are unresolved, so call-graph coverage is incomplete.
No patch, upstream history, CVE database, or sibling run was consulted; I could not determine whether the identified error-handling gap is already tracked upstream or intentional.
Exception classes, header-provider interfaces, servlet6/javax-portlet mirrors, and module POMs were only partially read; a defect there is possible but was not evidenced by the targeted searches.
The repository contains no test sources in this snapshot, so no test-derived evidence of the parsing behavior was available.

rejected_leads.lead: Part/file count is unlimited unless fileCountMax is explicitly set (AbstractFileUpload.fileCountMax = -1, check only in parseRequest at line 468).
rejected_leads.reason: Documented behavior of the 2.x API: the repository's own security-reports.xml (lines 61-76) states the new limit is disabled by default and must be explicitly configured (the CVE-2023-24998 option); the check exists and works for the list API. Not a distinct snapshot defect.

rejected_leads.lead: getItemIterator()/streaming API does not enforce fileCountMax at all, so the option silently has no effect there.
rejected_leads.reason: Appears to match upstream design where the option is enforced in parseRequest() only; the setter javadoc does not promise iterator enforcement, so this is a hardening/documentation gap rather than an evidenced vulnerability.

rejected_leads.lead: Predictable temporary file names (UID + sequential getUniqueId) allow TOCTOU/local-file tampering in shared temp directories (DiskFileItem.java:271, getUniqueId).
rejected_leads.reason: Requires a local attacker with write access to the repository directory; DiskFileItemFactory's javadoc explicitly documents this precondition and the mitigation (setPath to a non-public directory). Documented known limitation, not a remote-input vulnerability.

rejected_leads.lead: DiskFileItem.write(Path) uses Files.move(..., REPLACE_EXISTING) and may overwrite an existing target file.
rejected_leads.reason: The destination path is supplied by the application, not by request data; the library cannot validate the caller's policy. No attacker-controlled path derivation was found in the library itself.

rejected_leads.lead: DiskFileItem.isInMemory() dereferences dfos without a null check (NPE if the item was never written).
rejected_leads.reason: Reachable only via programmatic misuse (get()/isInMemory() before getOutputStream()); request-parsing always writes via getOutputStream(). No attacker-controlled trigger found.

rejected_leads.lead: AbstractFileUpload.parseEndOfLine throws unchecked IllegalStateException on malformed header termination.
rejected_leads.reason: readHeaders() guarantees the header section ends with CRLFCRLF before parsing, so the throw was not reachable from the parsing path in the source I inspected.

rejected_leads.lead: QuotedPrintableDecoder/RFC2231Utils write loops and fromHex table indexing could mis-decode.
rejected_leads.reason: Manual bounds analysis (HEX_DECODE index masked with 0x7F, truncation checks at QuotedPrintableDecoder.java:54) found no out-of-bounds or unbounded-write reachable from attacker input.

summary: Reviewed the Apache Commons FileUpload 2.0.0-M4-SNAPSHOT tree (99 files, 44 Java) with emphasis on the multipart parsing and header/parameter handling path: MultipartInput, FileItemInputIteratorImpl, AbstractFileUpload, FileItemInputImpl, DiskFileItem(-Factory), ParameterParser, RFC2231Utils, MimeUtils, QuotedPrintableDecoder, and the servlet/portlet adapters. The strongest source-evidenced defect is an error-handling gap in MimeUtils: attacker-controlled Content-Disposition parameter values containing an RFC 2047 encoded-word are Base64-decoded with java.util.Base64, which throws unchecked IllegalArgumentException on malformed input, while every caller on the request-parsing path catches only checked exceptions (ParseException/UnsupportedEncodingException/FileUploadException/IOException). A malformed value such as a truncated Base64 encoded-word in a part's filename/name parameter therefore escapes the library's documented FileUploadException/IOException contract as a raw RuntimeException. Other apparent leads (part-count limit only in the list API and disabled by default; predictable temp-file names; REPLACE_EXISTING writes) are either documented behavior or require preconditions I could not evidence, and are recorded as rejected leads.
